Heritage

Your people train you in one or two skills at no cost. Everyone is also trained in Jump, Run, Magic Defense, and Loyalty for free.

Class

Each preset spends all 330 attribute points and all 50 skill credits, and its skill list changes with your heritage.

Attributes

Six attributes share 330 points. Each starts at 10 and tops out at 100. Health is half your Endurance, Stamina equals it, and Mana equals Self.

Skills

Training adds 5 to a skill, specializing adds 10 more and makes it rise faster with use. You can only specialize now, during creation.

Skill goals

Name the values you want and the builder works out the cheapest way to get there, sharing attribute points across every goal at once, then says what level you need.

Suggested templates

Player-submitted builds from the Dark Majesty strategy guide, not from the client. Each spreads 330 attribute points; the credit figure is what its listed skills cost at creation under this era's table. Loading one sets the attributes and applies as many of its skills as 50 credits allow.

Advancement to level 126

Levelling earns skill points, which train new skills. Specializing is creation-only, so nothing here can be specialized later. Drag your level to see what you can afford.

Add a skill to the plan. Order matters — each is paid for in turn.

Experience targets

Set the values you are aiming for. Cost depends on your starting point, so a skill raised from a high base is far cheaper. Untrained skills can't be raised with experience at all. Each track is capped twice over: by the client's own limits — 190 points for an attribute, 208 for a trained skill, 220 for a specialized one in 1999 and 226 in 2001 — and by what a level 126 character could ever earn, whichever binds first. Each row shows its cap, and the plan as a whole stays inside that lifetime. The Skill goals section solves a harder version of the same question: a skill rises with the attributes beneath it, and attributes are shared, so raising Coordination serves every coordination skill at once. It finds the allocation by coordinate descent — scanning each attribute across its whole range with the others fixed, repeating until nothing moves — which against a brute-force search lands within about a tenth of a percent of the true optimum. Small hill-climbing steps do not work here, because a skill only shifts when the attribute sum crosses its divisor. The two rule sets differ in attribute costs and in specialized skills above the cut-off, where the Sybex guide's launch curve kept climbing and Turbine's December 2000 revision brought it down to roughly a tenth of trained cost. Below the cut-off the two agree exactly.

Where the sources disagree, the game data wins. Skill costs, formulas, descriptions, icons, class templates, attribute spreads and portraits are read from the retail client's own portal.dat (October 1999): the skill table at 0x0E000004 and the character-generation table at 0x0E000002, the character-creation text at 0x31000001 onward, and the starting areas and clothing in CharGen, the vital table at 0x0E000003 (which confirms Health = Endurance ÷ 2, Stamina = Endurance and Mana = Self), and the spell table at 0x0E00000E — 1,628 spells with their school, difficulty, mana cost, range, description and icon — Dark Majesty's fifteen new spell icons are read from its own archive, and the one spell whose icon is missing, the 1998 placeholder Cabbage of Doom, points at a texture that does not exist in any of the four builds — the portal and lifestone travel spells grouped for convenience, with the travel spells placed in the level tier matching their difficulty rather than the numeral in their name — a choice the components independently confirm, since Summon Portal I, II and III take the Silver, Gold and Pyreal Scarabs of tiers IV, V and VI rather than the Copper, Iron and Lead of I, II and III — stored with their text nibble-swapped. Attribute and vital icons are the client's own attribute-panel art (0x060002C4–C9 and 0x06000FA3–FA5), the same nine the game draws beside Strength through Mana. Comparing all four archives shows the art is stable except in three places, and the 1998 build gets its own: its Endurance and Coordination icons were later redrawn, and its Gharu'ndim emblem differs from the one used from 1999 onward. The eight class portraits and the remaining emblems and name banners are byte-identical in every build. One curiosity in that art: the Aluvian name plate reads ALLUVIAN with two Ls, a typo that survived from 1998 through to the 2001 expansion while the client's own text always spelled it with one. It is shown as drawn rather than corrected. The 330 attribute points, the 50 skill credits and each heritage's free skills are stored per heritage in that same table, so those totals are the client's too, not the manual's. That data is what the game actually ran on, so it supersedes both printed guides wherever they differ — and they do. The books get four class templates and four skill formulas wrong, and drop three skills from the Aluvian warrior. Every one of the client's 21 class and heritage combinations spends exactly 50 skill credits and 330 attribute points, which is the check that exposed those errors.

    
Four eras. Each setting is read from that build's own portal.dat. The three archives differ in format as much as in content: Preview 2 (October 1998) and Beta 0 (April 1999) index their files with 37 branch slots and 24-byte directory entries, retail uses 62 and 12; Preview 2 stores table text in plain bytes with 32-bit lengths, Beta 0 plain with 16-bit lengths, retail nibble-swapped with 16-bit lengths. Dark Majesty (September 2001) returns to retail's directory layout but stores skill text plainly and spell text nibble-swapped. They hold 8,171, 14,098, 17,794 and 30,397 files respectively. All 21 class and heritage combinations balance to exactly 50 credits in every era, which is the check that validates each dataset independently.

    
Dark Majesty renames every class again — Bow Hunter, Swashbuckler, Life Caster, War Mage, Wayfarer, Soldier — drops the Enchanter entirely, leaving seven, and rebuilds every attribute spread around values of 10 and 100. It keeps retail's 35 skills and costs but moves Magic Defense to ÷ 7, and gives each appraisal skill its own icon where retail shared one; those seven new icons are read from its own archive. Its spell table holds 2,287 entries against retail's 1,628, with difficulties raised again: Portal Tie 150, Summon Portal I 200. Opening a spell also shows how it differed between builds, where it did. That comparison is lopsided: 1,446 spells changed difficulty between Beta 0 and launch, against seven between launch and the 2001 expansion, and those seven are all travel spells being made harder — Portal Tie 100 to 150, Summon Portal I 150 to 200 — plus two evident data fixes, Blade Volley V and Rejuvenation Self VI both sitting at difficulty 10 where their tier demands 225 and 250. The only wording the expansion revised was weapon speed: Swift Killer and Leaden Weapon were flattened together from 25/40/60/80/100 to 20/30/40/50/60, the buff and its mirror moving in step. Each spell also shows what a cast costs. The casting time and the scarab's price come from the 2001 guide, which tables them by scarab — nothing at the first level, rising a second and roughly doubling in price at each one after, to five seconds and a thousand pyreals at the sixth. The other components are priced there too: ten pyreals a herb, five for a powdered gem, a reagent or a talisman, twenty-five a taper, with burdens of five for scarabs and tapers and four for the rest. The chance of burning a component is the spell's own, a field that runs from one per cent at the first level to thirty at the sixth; the guide names the mechanic — “each spell has a certain chance of burning one or more of its components, and if you fizzle a spell that chance increases” — without printing the numbers. Summon Portal III is the only spell in the game certain to burn one. Duration is not in the data at all. The 2001 guide tables it by level, and the asymmetry is the point: a buff holds for thirteen minutes to the fourth level and seventeen beyond it, while the same spell cast to hinder someone lasts seventy-five seconds at the first level and under nine minutes at the sixth, shorter on an attribute than on a skill. The guide's Power column is the difficulty field in the record, which its 854 Creature Enchantment spells confirm, and it shows the other half of that asymmetry: a debuff always costs twenty-five more Power than the buff of the same level, so hindering is dearer to cast and wears off sooner. Range comes from a field the guides never mention: it is zero for spells cast on yourself, 5 metres for those cast on another, 10 for item enchantments and 30 for projectiles, and Dark Majesty retunes it — item enchantments to 25, its new area spells to 4.5, matching their “waves outward from the caster”. The client stores metres and prints yards, dividing by 0.9144, so yards are shown here. No spell description states a distance, so the reading rests on that pattern rather than on text. About 80 spells, nearly all level I, have the field left at zero where their own higher tiers carry a value; those read “range not recorded” rather than repeating an apparent gap as fact. The Suggested templates section carries 17 player-submitted builds from the Dark Majesty strategy guide (Beth Loubet and Tuesday Frase, Sybex, 2002, ISBN 0782140599); every one spreads exactly 330 attribute points, which is how they were validated, though two — Extreme Dagger and Eighty-Two — list more skills than 50 credits can buy at creation. Dark Majesty grants an automatic skill credit at level 32. That is not an assumption: the same client file carries the credit-per-level schedule, and comparing the two clients shows level 32 is the single level where they differ — 37 credits by 126 against 1999's 36. The builder reads both schedules straight from the clients, so the level awards are no longer computed from the printed formula either. The Aun Ralirea toggle in the advancement section adds the quest's further credit from level 35, bringing the total to 88. Neither is read from the archive; level awards and quest rewards live on the server rather than in the client's tables.

    
Beta 0 sits between the other two. It keeps Preview 2's 32 skills, its eight classes (Adventurer, Healer, Rogue) and its six starting towns, but has already taken retail's Dagger formula, Missile Defense divisor, magic-school divisor, Appraise Magic Item divisor and two-skill heritage grants. It still has Preview 2's Magic Defense ÷ 6, Leadership and Loyalty on raw Self, and Healing at 8 to train. Its 1,622 spells carry a different difficulty curve: Portal Tie is 50 rather than 100, Summon Portal I is 70 rather than 150.

    
The 1998 Preview 2 setting is read from that build's own portal.dat, whose directory uses 37 branch slots and 24-byte entries rather than retail's 62 and 12, and whose tables store plain text with 32-bit lengths instead of retail's nibble-swapped 16-bit ones. Its five spells are developer placeholders whose records carry a school and an icon but no difficulty or mana, so the builder shows those as not recorded rather than inventing them. It has 32 skills rather than 35 — Alchemy, Cooking and Fletching did not exist — eight classes including Adventurer, Healer and Rogue, one free skill per heritage instead of two, six starting towns, and five placeholder spells. Fourteen skills changed between the builds: Magic Defense divided by 6 rather than 10, the magic schools by 6 rather than 4, Missile Defense by 3 rather than 5, Dagger keyed off Strength rather than Quickness, Leadership and Loyalty off raw Self, Healing cost 8 to train, and Loyalty was not yet free. Four skills carry the description “THIS SKILL IS NOT YET IMPLEMENTED.” Skill icons are byte-identical between the two builds, so the same art serves both; class descriptions have no equivalent in the preview and are carried over from retail; Dark Majesty has its own, keyed by each template's title id, and uses them. All 21 of its class and heritage combinations spend exactly 50 credits, the same check that validates the retail data.

    
The printed guides remain the source for what the client does not carry: the attribute and secondary experience tables, the character level curve, and the heritage and class descriptions — Asheron's Call Official Strategies & Secrets by Rusel DeMaria (Sybex Inc., November 1999, 344 pages, ISBN 0782126545), with the four skill classes described in the boxed game manual.

    
Two things the guides got wrong or left out are settled by the client: Unarmed Combat, absent from table 2.1 altogether, costs 6 to train and 6 to specialize; and the Aluvian warrior, printed 12 credits short, does train Appraise Armor, Appraise Weapon and Assess Creature.

    
Experience costs are read from the client after all, in file 0x0E000018 of the 1999 and 2001 archives — an earlier search missed it because it looked for the printed 1999 figures, which the shipped game does not use. That file holds the caps and the whole economy: attribute, secondary, trained and specialized costs and the level curve. The 1999 client caps read 190, 196, 208, 220 and 126, so the level cap and the training caps come from the game rather than from a community figure. Both clients share identical attribute, secondary, trained and level tables; they differ only in the specialized curve above its cut-off, which is precisely what the December 2000 update describes, and Dark Majesty's runs to 226 before dropping to ten points each. Nothing here is extrapolated any longer, and the printed tables are no longer used anywhere in the builder. The 1998 and 1999 Beta archives contain no such file — I scanned both for every known cost sequence and for any ascending run of the right shape — so those two eras fall back to the 1999 client's figures, which the note above the targets states.

    
One consequence worth stating plainly: the shipped 1999 client raises an attribute one point from base for 110 experience, not the 156 printed in the Sybex guide, and its level 126 total is 4,286,609,098 against the 4,286,609,097 my formula derived. The printed tables describe a build that did not ship. Total XP for a level is round(((level+5)5 − 7,776) ÷ 9), which reproduces all 49 rows of the guide's table 4.2 exactly; its prose claim that level 100 needs 66,254,067 points contradicts that table and is treated as a misprint. Attribute and secondary costs are transcribed from tables 4.3 and 4.4 — every row checked against a running-sum and a curve-smoothness test, with damaged rows read back off the page scans.

    
Trained and specialized costs come from Turbine's official guide update of 5 December 2000, which revises the specialization figures published in chapter 4 and runs to the caps: 208 points in a trained skill costs 4,203,819,496 XP and 226 in a specialized one costs 4,100,490,438, both just inside a level 126 character's lifetime. The 1999 setting restores the original curve as Sybex printed it, to 186 points; beyond that the table stops, so those rows are extended along its tail ratio.

    
What is missing, and why. Every spell here has its icon, description, formula and components; every skill its icon, description and proficiency interval; every class its portrait. Three things are absent, and all three are absent from the game rather than from this page. Cabbage of Doom, a 1998 placeholder, points at a texture that exists in none of the four archives. Portal Sending and Lifestone Sending in the 1999 Beta store formulas that cannot be anchored, since that build keeps components unscrambled and its ordinary numbers are indistinguishable from component ids. And the 1998 skill table is four bytes short: its final record, Creature Enchantment, declares 4,480 bytes where it needs 4,484, so the last field of the last skill runs off the end. Reading past the declared length finds zeros, so it was never written.

    
Spellings are the game's own. Text and art here are reproduced as the clients contain them, so a few oddities are theirs rather than mine. The gilded Aluvian name plate reads ALLUVIAN with two Ls, a typo in the art that survived from 1998 through to the 2001 expansion, while the same clients' text always spelled it with one. Two 1998 placeholder spells carry “Fixes the grevious injury” and “Loose stamina for giving someone else mana”. Nothing has been silently corrected: where a build wrote something a particular way, that is what you see.
